# Agents

The plugin registers primary agents, hidden slash-command agents, and subagents in OpenCode. Primary agents are selectable in the TUI; hidden slash-command agents run in primary mode but are activated through commands; subagents are intended for delegation through OpenCode's task mechanism or direct mention.

## Primary agents

Primary-agent role prompts depend on `primary.persona`; their names follow that persona only when `primary.useRoleName` is enabled.
Shared primary-agent prompt blocks are also shaped by configuration under `primary` in `squad.json`. See [Configuration](configuration.md).

| Professional name | Mythic role name | Model handler | Purpose                                                                        |
| ----------------- | ---------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `alpha`           | `atlas`          | `primary`     | First-line senior development, architecture, security, and consultation agent. |
| `architect`       | `daedalus`       | `primary`     | Architecture, RFC, and solution-design mode.                                   |
| `developer`       | `hephaestus`     | `primary`     | Focused software development mode.                                             |
| `orchestrator`    | `sisyphus`       | `coordinator` | Long-running execution and orchestration mode.                                 |

## Hidden squad command agents

These agents use short OpenCode display/registry names so the active agent appears as `Beta`, `Configuru`, or `Retitler` in the UI. Their stable configuration and model-routing scope remains `squad/*`.

| Display agent | Stable routing key | Model handler  | Command      | Purpose                                                                                      |
| ------------- | ------------------ | -------------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `beta`        | `squad/beta`       | `primary_beta` | `/beta`      | Lightweight second-opinion agent for critical alternative review of the current session.     |
| `configuru`   | `squad/configuru`  | `primary`      | `/configuru` | Hidden configuration agent used to inspect and safely modify opencode-squad/OpenCode config. |
| `retitler`    | `squad/retitler`   | `primary`      | `/retitler`  | Hidden session-title agent used to rename or propose names for the current session.          |

`beta` runs in primary mode only so `/beta` can access the current session context, but it is not a normal/selectable primary agent and is not part of the primary-agent inventory. `primary.persona`, `primary.useRoleName`, and execution-oriented `primary.userRequirements` / `primary.projectRequirements` do not reshape Beta the way they reshape normal primary agents.

`/beta` is registered only when both the normal primary route (Alpha/Atlas) and `squad/beta` resolve to concrete, different models. This avoids presenting Beta as an alternate LLM perspective when either side is implicit or both would run on the same model.

`retitler` can be shaped through `retitler.instructions` and `retitler.suggestions` in `squad.json`. See [Configuration](configuration.md).

## Codebase subagents

| Agent                     | Model handler   | Purpose                                                 |
| ------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `codebase/locator`        | `scout`         | Finds where files and symbols live. Returns paths only. |
| `codebase/analyzer`       | `code_analyzer` | Explains how code works with precise file references.   |
| `codebase/pattern-finder` | `code_analyzer` | Finds existing patterns and examples to model after.    |
| `codebase/coordinator`    | `coordinator`   | Coordinates multi-step codebase investigations.         |

## Code review subagents

| Agent                              | Model handler   | Purpose                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `code-review/coordinator`          | `coordinator`   | Orchestrates the code review pipeline.   |
| `code-review/analyzer`             | `code_analyzer` | Performs code review analysis.           |
| `code-review/reviewer-security`    | `code_analyzer` | Reviews security issues.                 |
| `code-review/reviewer-integrity`   | `code_analyzer` | Reviews correctness and robustness.      |
| `code-review/reviewer-performance` | `code_analyzer` | Reviews performance concerns.            |
| `code-review/reviewer-consistency` | `code_analyzer` | Reviews consistency and maintainability. |
| `code-review/scout`                | `scout`         | Gathers read-only review context.        |

## Project and documentation subagents

| Agent                       | Model handler             | Purpose                                            |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `project/developer`         | `developer`               | Implements scoped project changes.                 |
| `project/document-analyzer` | `small_document_analyzer` | Answers questions from project docs with evidence. |
| `project/document-writer`   | `big_document_analyzer`   | Disabled placeholder for future project docs work. |

## Council subagents

The Council coordinator prompt receives a registry-time table of the actual selected models for each member, after `models.agents`, default selectors, fallback, and availability-aware selection have been applied. Each Council member also receives its own resolved friendly model name in its identity block and footer, so the member's self-identification honestly reflects which model is currently behind the role rather than a hardcoded vendor claim.

| Agent                 | Default selector        | Purpose                                         |
| --------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `council/coordinator` | `@handler/coordinator`  | Synthesizes the Council of Five.                |
| `council/architect`   | `@provider/gpt`         | System design and structural reasoning.         |
| `council/guardian`    | `@provider/claude_opus` | Risk, safety, and critical review.              |
| `council/pragmatist`  | `@provider/glm`         | Practical delivery trade-offs.                  |
| `council/sage`        | `@provider/gemini_pro`  | Broad synthesis and reflective analysis.        |
| `council/visionary`   | `@provider/kimi`        | Alternative directions and future-facing ideas. |

## Research subagents

| Agent                 | Model handler | Purpose                                     |
| --------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `research/web-scout`  | `scout`       | Web research and source synthesis.          |
| `research/repo-scout` | `scout`       | External repo research via `external_repo`. |

## Model selection

Bundled agents route through `models.handlers` or direct `@provider/<name>` selectors, and can be overridden per registered agent name through `models.agents`. Beta intentionally uses the separate `primary_beta` handler so users can route it to a different model family than the normal `primary` handler. See [Configuration](configuration.md).

# Agents

`opencode-squad` registers a set of OpenCode agents for different kinds of work. Some are selectable as your current primary agent, some are hidden behind slash commands, and others are specialist subagents intended for delegated tasks.

## Agent types

| Type                 | Page                                        | How you use it                                                                   |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Primary agents       | [Primary agents](agents-primary.md)         | Select one as the current OpenCode agent for normal collaboration.               |
| Slash-command agents | [Slash-command agents](agents-commands.md)  | Invoke a hidden helper through commands such as `/beta` or `/retitler`.          |
| Specialist subagents | [Specialist subagents](agents-subagents.md) | Delegate focused work through OpenCode's task mechanism or direct agent mention. |
| Council agents       | [Council agents](agents-council.md)         | Ask for multi-perspective reasoning coordinated through the Council workflow.    |

## Names, display names, and routing keys

OpenCode shows agent display names in the UI, but `squad.json` model routing should prefer stable routing keys where they exist.

- Primary agents can change display names when `primary.persona` and `primary.useRoleName` are configured, but their stable routing keys remain `primary/*`.
- Hidden command agents use short display names such as `beta`, `configuru`, and `retitler`, while their stable routing keys are `squad/*`.
- Specialist subagents use their registry names directly, for example `codebase/analyzer` or `research/web-scout`.

See [Model routing](configuration-models.md) for provider pools, workload handlers, and per-agent overrides.

## Practical rule

Start with a primary agent. Use specialist subagents when the task has a narrow shape: codebase discovery, code review, web research, external repository analysis, or multi-agent reasoning. This keeps the primary conversation focused while still giving the work to a better-matched helper.

# Notes: src/agents

Scope: conventions for bundled OpenCode agents under `src/agents`.

## Layout

- Keep only `index.ts` at the `src/agents` root.
- Put agent implementations in group subdirectories such as `code-review`, `codebase`, `primary`, `project`, `squad`, or `web`.

## Factory convention

- Agent modules export named factories only; do not use default agent exports.
- Factory names mirror the registry naming style:
  - `code-review/reviewer-consistency` -> `createAgent_codeReview_reviewerConsistency`
  - `codebase/pattern-finder` -> `createAgent_codebase_patternFinder`
  - `primary/alpha` -> `createAgent_primary_alpha`
- Kebab-case path segments are converted to camelCase in factory names because agent groups and files use kebab-case on disk.
- `src/agents/index.ts` imports these factories and calls them inside `createBundledAgents(...)`.

## Why factories

- Agents must be built per runtime config because primary prompts, names, and model routing can depend on project-specific `squad.json`.
- Accept `SquadConfig` only where the agent currently needs config-derived behavior; keep other factories argument-free until needed.

## Adding an agent

- Choose the registry key/path first, following the existing group structure.
- Add the implementation under the matching group directory.
- Export `createAgent_<group>_<agentName>()` using the casing convention above.
- Register the factory call explicitly in `src/agents/index.ts`.

# Notes: src/tools

Scope: conventions for bundled OpenCode tools under `src/tools`.

## Layout

- Keep only `index.ts` at the `src/tools` root.
- Put each tool implementation in a subdirectory: `src/tools/<tool_name>/<tool_name>.ts`.
- Group related tools in a shared subdirectory when the tool IDs share a natural prefix, e.g. `review_context/*` or `scratchpad/*`.

## Factory convention

- Tool modules export named factories only; do not use `export default tool(...)`.
- Factory names use the tool ID in snake_case:
  - `sandbox_exec` -> `createTool_sandbox_exec`
  - `review_context_put` -> `createTool_review_context_put`
  - `configuru_manual_get` -> `createTool_configuru_manual_get`
- `src/tools/index.ts` imports these factories and calls them inside `createTools(...)`.

## Why factories

- Tools must be built per plugin/project context because `squad.json` can be project-specific.
- Pass project-specific dependencies through factory parameters, e.g. normalized project root, loaded `SquadConfig`, config diagnostics, or OpenCode client access.

## Adding a tool

- Choose the runtime tool ID first; keep it snake_case.
- Create `src/tools/<tool_id>/<tool_id>.ts` or add it to an existing grouped directory.
- Export `createTool_<tool_id>()` or `createTool_<tool_id>(context)`.
- Register the factory call explicitly in `src/tools/index.ts`.

# Notes: src/tools/configuru

Scope: this file describes only the configuru tooling under this directory.

## Manuals (./manuals)

- Markdown files only. The basename without `.md` is the page key.
- YAML frontmatter is required and `description` is mandatory.
- The frontmatter parser is a minimal subset, not a full YAML implementation. It supports only:
  - one `key: value` pair per line
  - `seeAlso` as inline list `[a, b]` or single value `a`
  - block list form (newline + `- a`) is NOT supported
- `tier` accepts only string values: `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"`, `"3"`, `"reference"`. Unknown values throw at load.
- No caching. Every `manual_list` / `manual_get` call rereads the directory.

## Content rules for the bundled manuals

- Examples must use neutral placeholders such as `<preferred-provider/gpt-strong>` or `<provider/model-strong>`. Concrete vendor prefixes (e.g. `openai/`, `anthropic/`, `opencode/`, `baseten/`) belong in `configuru_models_get` output, never in a manual.
- `init.md` and `squad-recipes.md` are integrity-checked by tests for the rule above; treat any failing check as a content bug, not a test bug.

# Agent Skills

Skills live as one folder per skill with a `SKILL.md` file:

```txt
.opencode/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md
```

Frontmatter:

```md
---
name: my-skill
description: Use when a concise condition matches this skill.
---
```

`name` must match the folder name and use lowercase hyphen-separated characters. `description` is required for discovery.

Control skill access with permission:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "skill": {
      "*": "allow",
      "internal-*": "deny"
    }
  }
}
```

# opencode-squad

OpenCode plugin that packages the Squad agent and tool runtime.

> [!WARNING]
> **Early alpha:** `opencode-squad` is still evolving quickly. Expect breaking changes in configuration, bundled agents, tools, commands, and runtime behavior before a stable release.
> For production or shared setups, pin a concrete package version instead of using `@latest`.

## What it provides

`opencode-squad` extends OpenCode with:

- primary agents with stable routing keys such as `primary/alpha`, `primary/architect`, `primary/developer`, and `primary/orchestrator`
- hidden slash-command agents such as `beta` for `/beta` second-opinion reviews, with stable `squad/*` routing keys for configuration
- specialized subagents for codebase analysis, code review, project documentation, web research, and council-style reasoning
- custom tools for container inspection, isolated execution, external repository research, SearXNG search, scratchpad state, handoffs, review context, file inspection, and diagnostics
- bundled container definitions used by containerized tools
- strict JSON configuration through `squad.json`

## Local usage

```json
{
  "plugin": ["/absolute/path/to/opencode-squad"]
}
```

Or with inline plugin options:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    [
      "/absolute/path/to/opencode-squad",
      {
        "models": {
          "providers": {
            "gpt": ["openai/gpt-5.5", "opencode/gpt-5.2-codex"]
          },
          "handlers": {
            "primary": "@provider/gpt"
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  ]
}
```

For npm/package usage, add the package name instead of a local path:

```json
{
  "plugin": ["@geck-dev/opencode-squad@latest"]
}
```

## Configuration

The plugin reads `squad.json` from:

1. global OpenCode config dir: `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/squad.json` or `~/.config/opencode/squad.json`
2. project config: `<project>/.opencode/squad.json`
3. plugin tuple options in `opencode.json` — highest priority

See [`docs/dev/configuration.md`](docs/dev/configuration.md).

For editor validation in `squad.json`, use the raw schema URL:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/geck-dev/opencode-squad/main/schema/squad.schema.json"
}
```

Do not use GitHub's `/blob/` URL for `$schema`; it returns an HTML page, not raw JSON.

## Documentation

- Public main manual: <https://geck.dev/opencode-squad/>
- Internal architecture and development docs: [`docs/dev`](docs/dev)
- [Architecture](docs/dev/architecture.md)
- [Agents](docs/dev/agents.md)
- [Tools](docs/dev/tools.md)
- [Containers](docs/dev/containers.md)

```bash
bun install
bun run check
```

Build the optional static manual into the ignored root `manual/` directory:

```bash
bun run manual:build
```

# Architecture

`opencode-squad` is an OpenCode plugin package. It registers bundled agents through OpenCode's plugin `config` hook and exposes custom tools through the plugin `tool` registry.

## Startup flow

```text
OpenCode starts
  -> loads opencode-squad plugin module
  -> reads and merges squad.json sources
  -> configures runtime model/path settings
  -> hydrates directory-scoped local model availability cache
  -> dynamically imports agents, commands, and tools
  -> registers OpenCode agents
  -> registers OpenCode slash commands
  -> registers custom tools
  -> schedules background model availability refresh
```

The dynamic import step is intentional. Agent modules declare routing metadata during module initialization, while `buildAgentRegistry()` resolves final model strings from the loaded config plus a directory-scoped local availability snapshot.

## Important modules

| Path                          | Responsibility                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/index.ts`                | Plugin entrypoint and OpenCode hook registration.                   |
| `src/lib/config/`             | `squad.json` defaults, loading, merge logic, and runtime accessors. |
| `src/lib/types/config.ts`     | Canonical `SquadConfig` type and config value constants.            |
| `src/lib/models/resolver.ts`  | Resolves provider, handler, and agent model selectors to model IDs. |
| `src/lib/utils/paths.ts`      | Resolves config, data, and bundled container asset paths.           |
| `src/agents/index.ts`         | Bundled agent registry.                                             |
| `src/agents/primary/_shared/` | Shared primary-agent prompt blocks and persona/name selectors.      |
| `src/commands/index.ts`       | Bundled slash command registry and command contributions.           |
| `src/tools/index.ts`          | Custom tool registry.                                               |

## Configuration layering

The normalized configuration is produced from:

1. built-in defaults
2. global `squad.json`
3. project `.opencode/squad.json`
4. plugin tuple options

Later sources override earlier sources except machine-local fields such as `paths.dataDir` and `paths.containersDir`, which are honored only from trusted global `squad.json`. See [Configuration](configuration.md) and [Security](security.md).

## Runtime state

Stateful tools use the configured data directory:

1. `$OPENCODE_DATA_DIR`
2. `paths.dataDir`, when configured in the trusted global `squad.json`
3. `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/data` or `~/.config/opencode/data`

This currently affects scratchpad, handoff, review-context tools, external-repository research tools, and the available-model cache used by model routing. Availability cache entries are scoped by OpenCode directory and persisted under `agents/available-models/<scope-hash>.json` to avoid cross-project model availability pollution in long-lived OpenCode processes.

External-repository research tools keep shared bare mirrors under `external-repos/mirrors/<repo-hash>.git` and per-project worktrees plus registry state under `external-repos/projects/<project-hash>/`. Agents address those repositories by alias through `external_repo_*` tools rather than relying on direct filesystem paths.

## Model routing

Bundled agents declare internal model routing metadata during module initialization. `buildAgentRegistry()` resolves that metadata into static OpenCode `model` strings from an explicit resolution context containing the loaded `squad.json` config and the current directory's cached OpenCode provider availability snapshot. Live provider availability refresh is scheduled after plugin startup to avoid re-entering OpenCode provider discovery during plugin initialization. The resolver expands selectors in this order:

1. `models.agents[agentName]`, when registry-time routing resolves the bundled agent metadata
2. the agent's default `@handler/<name>` or `@provider/<name>` selector
3. `models.fallback`

Provider and handler keys are open-ended user aliases. Built-in constants only document the bundled defaults; they are not a validation whitelist.

With the default `models.selection` policy, resolver picks the first currently available concrete model from the expanded selector, then tries `models.fallback`, and degrades to configured order when availability data is unavailable or no configured candidate is known as available.

After all agent models are resolved, `buildAgentRegistry()` performs a second pass over registered prompt strings and replaces internal placeholders. Two placeholders are supported:

- `{{SQUAD_AGENT_MODEL:<agent>}}` renders the raw resolved model ID (for example `opencode/claude-opus-4-6`). Used by the Council coordinator's member table for honest debugging.
- `{{SQUAD_AGENT_FRIENDLY_MODEL:<agent>}}` renders a humanized model name (for example `Claude Opus 4 6`) by stripping the provider prefix and formatting tokens. Used by Council member identity blocks and footers so each member sees the actual model it runs as, not a hardcoded vendor claim.

Both placeholders go through the same prompt-injection guard. Prompt-rendered model IDs are constrained to an inert model-ID character set; nonconforming values render as `untrusted-model` (raw) or `Untrusted Model` (friendly).

## Container assets

Containerized tools use definitions from:

1. `paths.containersDir`, when configured in the trusted global `squad.json`
2. OpenCode config dir overrides, when present
3. bundled package assets under `containers/`

SearXNG does not ship or persist a static secret. The helper generates a runtime secret and passes it to Compose through the environment.

# Configuration

The plugin configuration file is named `squad.json`.

## Resolution order

Configuration is merged in this order:

1. Global config: `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/squad.json` or `~/.config/opencode/squad.json`
2. Project config: `<project>/.opencode/squad.json`
3. Plugin tuple options from `opencode.json`

Later sources override earlier sources.

If the global config path is the same file as a project config candidate (for example `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.opencode` while OpenCode is started from `$HOME`), that file is loaded only as global config. This prevents machine-local/user-only settings from being reported as invalid project settings.

Exception: machine-local fields such as `paths.dataDir` and `paths.containersDir` are honored only from global `squad.json`. Project config and plugin tuple options cannot override local machine paths; unsafe values are ignored with a security warning.

Exception: `primary.userRequirements` is honored only from global `squad.json`, while `primary.projectRequirements` is honored only from project `.opencode/squad.json` files. Values from the wrong source are ignored with a warning.

## Supported fields

### `retitler.instructions`

Additional prompt instructions for the hidden `/retitler` session-title agent.

Supported forms:

1. a single string
2. a string array

Instructions from later config sources are appended after earlier sources. Use this for project-specific naming standards such as ticket prefixes, language, or emoji/title style.

Example:

```json
"retitler": {
  "instructions": [
    "Use `ABC-123 — summary` when a ticket ID appears.",
    "Prefer Czech titles unless the task is explicitly English-only."
  ]
}
```

Command arguments still apply after configured instructions, so a user can add one-off guidance such as:

```txt
/retitler Use a robot emoji prefix
```

### `retitler.suggestions`

When `false` or omitted, `/retitler` chooses one title and renames the current session.

When `true`, `/retitler` proposes three options by default instead of immediately renaming:

1. short
2. concise standard
3. more expressive

If the command text explicitly asks to apply or choose a title, the agent may still rename the session directly.

### `primary.userTraits`

User trait map or string list rendered into the shared primary-agent `# USER` prompt block.

Object keys may be written in lower-case for readable configuration. During prompt rendering, the first key character is uppercased. Each object entry is emitted in insertion order as:

```md
- **<Key>:** <Value>
```

Array entries are emitted as simple bullets:

```md
- <Value>
```

Prompt-facing values are escaped during rendering; see [Prompt-text escaping](#prompt-text-escaping).

With the example configuration above, the rendered prompt section stays:

```md
# USER

I am the owner of the hardware you run on and where I want to build with you.
I am the one who can switch you between **modes**, your roles.

## TRAITS

- **Seniority:** We communicate senior-to-senior. No explaining basics unless I ask. Get to the point.
- **Language:** Conversation in Czech. Code and technical terms in English.
- **Environment:** I am a senior dev, running Linux (Bazzite/Fedora based), using Docker/Podman.
```

### `primary.userRequirements`

User-defined rules rendered as a conditional top-level `<user_requirements>` prompt block after the built-in primary-agent `<general_rules>` block. This field is honored only from global `squad.json`; project config and plugin tuple options are ignored with a warning.

### `primary.projectRequirements`

Project-defined rules rendered as a conditional top-level `<project_requirements>` prompt block after `<user_requirements>` when present, or after `<general_rules>` otherwise. This field is honored only from project `.opencode/squad.json` files; global config and plugin tuple options are ignored with a warning.

These requirements are for normal selectable primary agents. The hidden `/beta` command agent is registered as `beta`, uses `squad/beta` as its stable routing key, and runs in primary mode only to access current session context; it does not inherit execution-oriented user or project requirements like normal primary agents.

Both fields support the same forms:

1. flat string array
2. object of section name -> string array
3. object of section name -> string map rendered as `- **<Key>:** <Value>`

Requirement section names, map keys, and values use the same prompt-text escaping as `primary.userTraits`; see [Prompt-text escaping](#prompt-text-escaping).

Flat user requirements example:

```json
"primary": {
  "userRequirements": [
    "ALWAYS write code so that another senior developer can understand it quickly without guessing intent",
    "ALWAYS prefer the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem and avoid unnecessary abstraction"
  ]
}
```

Sectioned project requirements example:

```json
"primary": {
  "projectRequirements": {
    "testing": [
      "Cover complex methods by tests",
      "Run tests after finishing"
    ],
    "coding": {
      "clarity": "Write readable code.",
      "security": "Treat input as untrusted."
    }
  }
}
```

Rendered result when both fields are configured:

```text
<general_rules>
# GENERAL RULES

- ALWAYS communicate with subagents (tasks) only in English
- ALWAYS write notes and documentation only in English (unless the user says otherwise)
</general_rules>

<user_requirements>
# USER REQUIREMENTS

User-defined rules. They take precedence over GENERAL RULES on conflict.

- ALWAYS write code so that another senior developer can understand it quickly without guessing intent
- ALWAYS prefer the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem and avoid unnecessary abstraction
</user_requirements>

<project_requirements>
# PROJECT REQUIREMENTS

Rules for the current project. They take precedence over GENERAL RULES and USER REQUIREMENTS on conflict.

## TESTING
- Cover complex methods by tests
- Run tests after finishing

## CODING
- **Clarity:** Write readable code.
- **Security:** Treat input as untrusted.
</project_requirements>
```

### Prompt-text escaping

Prompt-facing configuration values are rendered as data inside their intended prompt section. This applies to `primary.userTraits`, `primary.userRequirements`, `primary.projectRequirements`, and future configuration fields that use the shared primary prompt helpers.

During prompt rendering:

- literal `<`, `>`, and `&` characters render as entities,
- embedded newline characters, including Unicode line separators, render as the literal two-character sequence `\n`.

This keeps normal prose unchanged while preventing config-derived values from closing XML-like prompt blocks or forging extra markdown sections. Keep JSON values in their natural readable form; do not pre-escape them manually.

Example:

```text
Input:  Rule </user> & <safety_protocol>
        ## fake section
Render: - Rule </user> & <safety_protocol>\n## fake section
```

### `primary.identity`

Controls the primary agent identity framing.

Allowed values:

- `"neutral"`
- `"jarvis"`

Default: `"neutral"`

### `primary.persona`

Controls role persona framing for the primary agent modes.

Allowed values:

- `"mythic"`
- `"professional"`

Default: `"professional"`

This setting controls the system prompt role block used by primary agents.

- `"professional"` uses neutral, non-mythological role framing.
- `"mythic"` uses mythology-inspired role framing such as `atlas`, `daedalus`, `hephaestus`, and `sisyphus`.

This changes primary-agent role framing only. Primary-agent names follow `primary.useRoleName`, while subagent names and internal model handlers stay unchanged.

### `primary.useRoleName`

Controls whether primary-agent display names should follow `primary.persona`.

Allowed values:

- `true`
- `false`

Default: `false`

When `false`, primary agents keep their stable professional display names such as `alpha`, `architect`, `developer`, and `orchestrator` even when `primary.persona` is `"mythic"`.

When `true`, primary agents use persona-derived display names. With `primary.persona` set to `"mythic"`, those names are `atlas`, `daedalus`, `hephaestus`, and `sisyphus`.

### `primary.outputIcons`

Controls prompt icon style.

Allowed values:

- `"emoji"`
- `"nerdfont"`
- `false`

Default: `"emoji"`

### `models.providers`

Logical model provider pools. Each key is user-defined and maps to one or more concrete OpenCode model IDs such as `openai/gpt-5.4` or `opencode/kimi-k2.5`.

Provider keys are not whitelisted. Bundled defaults use names such as `gpt`, `claude_opus`, `gemini_pro`, `kimi`, and `glm`, but users may define their own aliases.

Selectors can be written as a single string or as a string array:

```json
"providers": {
  "gpt": ["openai/gpt-5.4", "opencode/gpt-5.2-codex"],
  "local": "ollama/qwen3-coder"
}
```

Provider entries may also reference other providers or handlers. Cyclic references are skipped during resolution.

### `models.handlers`

Workload-level model routing used by bundled agents. Handler keys are not whitelisted; bundled agents use constants such as `primary`, `primary_beta`, `developer`, `coordinator`, `code_analyzer`, `vision`, and `scout` as defaults.

Handlers may reference providers with `@provider/<name>` or concrete model IDs directly:

```json
{
  "handlers": {
    "primary_beta": "@provider/alternative-strong-model",
    "code_analyzer": ["@provider/gpt", "@provider/claude_sonnet"],
    "vision": "@provider/gemini_pro"
  }
}
```

### `models.agents`

Per-agent overrides keyed by the registered agent name or a bundled stable routing key, for example `codebase/analyzer`, `project/developer`, or `council/guardian`.

Primary agents additionally support stable routing keys that do not change with `primary.useRoleName`: `primary/alpha`, `primary/architect`, `primary/developer`, and `primary/orchestrator`. Display-name keys such as `alpha` or `atlas` are accepted as aliases, but stable keys take precedence.

Hidden squad command agents use short OpenCode display names (`beta`, `configuru`, `retitler`) and stable `squad/*` model-routing keys (`squad/beta`, `squad/configuru`, `squad/retitler`). Prefer the stable keys in shared config. Display-name aliases are accepted, but stable keys take precedence. `/beta` is registered only when both the normal primary route (Alpha/Atlas) and `squad/beta` resolve to concrete, different models.

Agent selectors may reference either providers or handlers:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "primary/alpha": "@provider/gpt",
    "squad/beta": "@handler/primary_beta",
    "squad/retitler": "@handler/primary",
    "codebase/analyzer": "@handler/code_analyzer",
    "council/guardian": ["@provider/claude_opus", "@handler/code_analyzer"]
  }
}
```

Agent overrides are evaluated before the bundled agent's default handler/provider selector.

### `models.fallback`

Final fallback selector used when an agent override, provider, or handler resolves to no concrete model IDs.

```json
"fallback": "@provider/gpt"
```

### `models.selection`

Model selection policy after provider/handler references are expanded.

Default:

```json
"selection": {
  "availability": "opencode",
  "strategy": "first_available",
  "cacheTtlMs": 1800000,
  "refreshTimeoutMs": 3000
}
```

When `availability` is `"opencode"` and `strategy` is `"first_available"`, the plugin uses cached OpenCode provider metadata to select the first configured candidate that is currently available. Provider metadata is refreshed in the background after plugin startup and cached per OpenCode directory under the plugin data directory for later registry builds.

Resolution order:

1. first available candidate from the agent/handler/provider selector
2. first available candidate from `models.fallback`
3. first configured candidate from the selector when no availability data matches
4. first configured candidate from `models.fallback`

Set `strategy` to `"first_configured"` or `availability` to `"none"` to ignore availability data and use configured order directly.

### `paths.dataDir`

Data directory used by stateful tools such as scratchpad, handoffs, and review context.

Resolution priority:

1. `$OPENCODE_DATA_DIR`
2. `paths.dataDir` from global `squad.json`
3. `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/data` or `~/.config/opencode/data`

### `paths.containersDir`

Optional override directory for container definitions.

For safety, this setting is honored only from the trusted global `squad.json` configuration file. Project `.opencode/squad.json` files and plugin tuple options cannot override container asset locations.

When unset, the plugin first checks OpenCode config dir overrides and then falls back to bundled container assets shipped with the package.

## Design note

The first version intentionally uses strict JSON only. JSONC/YAML compatibility can be added later behind the same normalized config model.

See [Security](security.md) for source trust rules. Future configuration expansion is tracked in [Roadmap](roadmap.md).

# Containers

`opencode-squad` uses local Docker/Podman containers for two different purposes:

1. helper execution containers used by `sandbox_exec` and `chroot_exec`
2. the local SearXNG service used by `searxng_search` and `searxng_engines`

This document describes the helper container lifecycle. SearXNG uses a Compose-based flow and is covered separately in [Tools](tools.md).

## Runtime detection

The runtime layer detects container tooling in this order:

1. Podman
2. Docker

Runtime-specific behavior is centralized in `src/lib/runtime/container.ts`. For example, image existence checks use:

- Podman: `podman image exists <image>`
- Docker: `docker image inspect <image>`

This avoids assuming that Podman-only commands exist in Docker.

The runtime layer also classifies the selected engine as `rootless`, `rootful`, or `unknown`:

- Podman reads `host.security.rootless` from `podman info --format json`.
- Docker checks whether `docker info --format '{{json .SecurityOptions}}'` reports a rootless security option.

Rootless engines keep the default container-root behavior because writes to bind mounts are mapped back to the user running the engine. Rootful engines run helper containers and command executions as the host UID/GID when Node exposes those values. This prevents root-owned files from being created in bind-mounted project or sandbox directories.

## Helper tools

| Tool           | Container name scope | Mount                     | Image base name              |
| -------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `sandbox_exec` | OpenCode session     | session data → `/sandbox` | `localhost/opencode-sandbox` |
| `chroot_exec`  | project root         | project root → `/chroot`  | `localhost/opencode-runtime` |

`sandbox_exec` persists files written to `/sandbox` because that path is backed by plugin data storage. `chroot_exec` mounts the real project root read-write at `/chroot`; changes there are changes to the working tree.

Helper images provide dedicated home directories outside their mounted workdirs:

- `chroot_exec`: `/home/chroot`
- `sandbox_exec`: `/home/sandbox`

For rootful runtimes, the helper process receives `HOME` pointing at the relevant dedicated directory while still using `/chroot` or `/sandbox` as its working directory. This keeps incidental user-cache files out of the project mount.

Container filesystem changes outside mounted paths are temporary. If a package is installed into the running helper container, that installation survives only while the helper container is reused. It is not guaranteed to survive idle TTL cleanup, image rebuilds, or manual container removal. Durable runtime dependencies should be added to the relevant `Containerfile`.

## Image revisions

Helper images are not addressed internally by a static `:latest` tag. The plugin derives a short revision from the active `Containerfile` content plus an internal schema salt:

```text
revision = sha256(Containerfile bytes + schema salt).slice(0, 12)
```

The final image reference is:

```text
<base-name>:cf-<revision>
```

Examples:

```text
localhost/opencode-sandbox:cf-56c4e10d9793
localhost/opencode-runtime:cf-b863376a811e
```

When a bundled or configured `Containerfile` changes, the computed revision changes. The next matching tool invocation builds the new image revision automatically.

## Managed labels

Images and helper containers created by the plugin are labeled so cleanup can distinguish plugin-owned resources from unrelated user containers/images.

Common labels:

```text
opencode-squad.managed=true
opencode-squad.tool=sandbox_exec|chroot_exec
opencode-squad.image-revision=<revision>
```

Container identity labels:

```text
opencode-squad.session-hash=<hash>  # sandbox_exec
opencode-squad.project-hash=<hash>  # chroot_exec
```

Cleanup must only remove resources that match the expected managed labels and identity.

## Tool invocation flow

At a high level, each helper tool invocation follows this sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Tool invocation] --> B[Run opportunistic expired-container cleanup]
    B --> C[Compute Containerfile revision]
    C --> D{Desired image exists?}
    D -- No --> E[Build desired managed image]
    E --> F[Post-build prune obsolete images]
    D -- Yes --> G[Skip image prune]
    F --> H[Inspect existing helper container]
    G --> H
    H --> I{Managed labels and revision match?}
    I -- Yes --> J[Reuse running container]
    I -- No --> K[Remove stale container]
    K --> L[Start new managed container]
    J --> M[Touch lease before exec]
    L --> M
    M --> N[Execute requested command]
    N --> O{Command timed out?}
    O -- No --> P[Touch lease after exec]
    O -- Yes --> Q[Return timeout error]
    P --> R[Return command output and exit code]
```

If the `Containerfile` changes while an old helper container is still running, the next invocation of that same tool computes the new revision, builds the new image if needed, rejects the old container because its revision label no longer matches, removes it, starts a new container from the new image, and executes the requested command in the new container.

Other tools are not interrupted by this process. For example, rebuilding `sandbox_exec` does not stop a still-valid `chroot_exec` container.

## Container idle TTL

Persistent helper containers are reused for performance, but they are not intended to live forever.

The plugin stores sliding idle lease records under the resolved data directory:

```text
data/containers/leases/*.json
```

Default helper TTL:

```text
8 hours
```

Environment override:

```text
OPENCODE_CONTAINER_HELPER_TTL_MS=<milliseconds>
```

Each helper tool invocation touches the matching lease before command execution and, when the command returns without a tool-level timeout, touches it again after execution. This keeps the lease fresh for both successful and non-zero commands. Expired helpers are removed opportunistically at the start of later `sandbox_exec` or `chroot_exec` invocations.

Important consequence: this is not a background timer. If no container-backed tool runs after a lease expires, the expired container can remain running until the next tool invocation or manual cleanup.

Lease records survive normal OpenCode restarts because they are stored in the plugin data directory. After restart, the next helper tool invocation can still remove expired plugin-managed containers from previous processes.

## Obsolete image pruning

Older managed image revisions are pruned only after a new image revision is built successfully.

Normal tool invocations do not scan image history. The image prune flow is intentionally post-build only:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Desired image missing] --> B[Build new revision]
    B --> C{Build successful?}
    C -- No --> D[Return build error]
    C -- Yes --> E[List managed images for same tool]
    E --> F[Skip current revision]
    F --> G{Old image used by any container?}
    G -- Yes --> H[Keep image]
    G -- No --> I[Remove old image]
```

An old image is removed only if all of these are true:

- it is labeled `opencode-squad.managed=true`
- it belongs to the same tool label
- its revision differs from the newly built revision
- no existing container reports that image reference as its image

This preserves older image revisions while an older helper container is still using them. Once those containers are gone and a later image build occurs, obsolete unused image revisions can be removed.

## Diagnostics and timeouts

Container command execution is wrapped by the runtime diagnostics layer. Failures include:

- selected runtime
- full command
- duration
- timeout
- exit code/signal
- stdout/stderr when available

Useful environment variables:

```text
OPENCODE_CONTAINER_DEBUG=1
OPENCODE_CONTAINER_TIMEOUT_MS=120000
OPENCODE_CONTAINER_BUILD_TIMEOUT_MS=900000
OPENCODE_CONTAINER_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS=300000
OPENCODE_CONTAINER_HELPER_TTL_MS=28800000
```

`OPENCODE_CONTAINER_DEBUG=1` adds collected phase diagnostics to successful tool output. Without debug mode, diagnostics are primarily returned on errors.

## Safety model

The container lifecycle code is deliberately conservative:

- never remove resources without plugin ownership labels
- validate tool identity and project/session identity before removing helper containers
- prune images only after a successful newer image build
- do not prune images that are still used by any container
- keep cleanup opportunistic rather than introducing a background daemon

This keeps normal tool use fast while still preventing stale helper containers and obsolete image revisions from accumulating indefinitely.

The public manual source lives under `docs/manual`. The static site builder lives under `docs/site` and emits generated HTML into the root `manual/` directory:

```bash

The generated `manual/` directory is ignored by Git. The builder writes a sentinel file before cleaning output and refuses to remove an existing `manual/` directory without that sentinel.

Clean generated output with:

```

If the manual is published to a private static server, serve the generated `manual/` directory with a normal static file server such as Caddy, nginx, or an internal file server. For rsync-style publishing, run a dry-run before using destructive flags such as `--delete`.

# Security Model

`opencode-squad` treats configuration as input with different trust levels. Project repositories can provide configuration, so not every `squad.json` source is allowed to modify local machine resources.

## Trust boundaries

| Source                                                                                     | Trust level | Allowed scope                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Global `squad.json` (`$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/squad.json` or `~/.config/opencode/squad.json`) | trusted     | Full user-controlled local machine configuration. |
| Project `.opencode/squad.json`                                                             | untrusted   | Project and agent behavior only.                  |
| Plugin tuple options                                                                       | untrusted   | Same policy as project config.                    |

Project config may customize project behavior. Global config may customize local machine resources.

## Model routing fields

Model routing fields (`models.providers`, `models.handlers`, `models.agents`, and `models.fallback`) are intentionally project-configurable so repositories can tune agent behavior for their workload.

Because these fields select remote model IDs, review project `.opencode/squad.json` before using untrusted repositories. A project can route prompts and code context to any provider/model that is already available in the user's OpenCode environment. Keep sensitive or policy-critical model routing in trusted global `squad.json` when repository-level overrides are not desired.

## Prompt-facing config fields

Prompt-facing primary fields (`primary.userTraits`, `primary.userRequirements`, and `primary.projectRequirements`) are rendered into agent prompts and may be influenced by project repositories where their source policy allows it.

To reduce prompt-structure injection risk, config-derived prompt text is escaped before it is embedded into XML-like prompt blocks. Literal `<`, `>`, and `&` render as entities, and embedded newline characters, including Unicode line separators, render as the literal two-character sequence `\n`. This keeps configured text inside its intended prompt section instead of allowing values such as `</project_requirements>` or `<safety_protocol>` to close or forge prompt blocks.

This escaping protects prompt structure; it does not make project configuration semantically trusted. Review untrusted project `.opencode/squad.json` before relying on its instructions.

## Machine-local fields

Machine-local fields affect host paths, persistent writes, or executable assets. They are accepted only from global `squad.json`.

Current machine-local fields:

- `paths.dataDir` — base directory for stateful plugin writes such as scratchpad, handoff, and review context data.
- `paths.containersDir` — base directory for container definitions and Compose assets.

If project config or plugin tuple options set these fields, the values are ignored, a security warning is logged, and a delayed TUI toast notifies the user. The plugin continues with safe configuration from defaults and trusted global config.

## Executable assets

Container definitions are executable assets. A repository must never be able to redirect `sandbox_exec`, `chroot_exec`, or SearXNG to repo-controlled container files through project configuration.

Only global `paths.containersDir` can redirect container assets through `squad.json`. OpenCode config directory asset overrides remain user-controlled local files and are checked before bundled package assets when `paths.containersDir` is unset.

## Write destinations

Persistent write destinations are trusted-only unless a future feature explicitly constrains them to a safe project-local directory controlled by the plugin.

Do not add arbitrary project-configurable write paths. If project-local state is needed, prefer a boolean or enum that resolves internally to a fixed path such as `<project>/.opencode/data`.

## Error and warning policy

- Malformed JSON and unsupported config fields are fatal during config loading.
- Trusted-only fields from untrusted sources are non-fatal: ignore the value, log the issue, and show a warning toast.
- Security warnings must identify the source and field path so the user can move the setting to global `squad.json`.

## Rules for future config fields

Every new config field must declare its trust policy before implementation:

1. Is it safe from project config?
2. Does it affect host paths, writes, process execution, networking, credentials, or executable assets?
3. Should invalid values fail fast or degrade with a warning?
4. Does documentation and schema describe the source policy?

When in doubt, treat the field as trusted-global-only.

## Stateful tool data

Scratchpad, handoff, and review-context tools store data under the resolved data directory:

1. `$OPENCODE_DATA_DIR`
2. `paths.dataDir` from trusted global `squad.json`
3. `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/data` or `~/.config/opencode/data`

Handoffs are stored in `<dataDir>/handoffs` as markdown files with frontmatter. Tool output exposes the stable `hash`, title, and creation time; filenames remain an internal storage detail. Filenames include a six-character handoff hash prefix and a deterministic five-character project hash derived from the project path so lookup and current-project listing can narrow candidates before reading file contents. Each handoff also stores `projectHash` and `projectPath` in frontmatter for verification.

External repository tools store per-project registries and checkout state under `<dataDir>/external-repos`. Mirror caches are shared across projects by repository URL hash, while worktrees and `registry.json` files are scoped by a deterministic hash of the current project root:

```text
<dataDir>/external-repos/
  mirrors/<repo_hash>.git
  projects/<project_hash>/registry.json
  projects/<project_hash>/<alias>/worktree
```

The agent-facing API uses aliases instead of physical paths. `external_repo_add` prepares the mirror/worktree, records the exact commit, and suggests follow-up `external_repo_search`, `external_repo_read`, and `external_repo_tree` calls. `external_repo_update` is explicit so reference state does not unexpectedly change during analysis.

`external_repo_search` keeps output compact while preserving orientation. It reports exact match counts up to 100 matches and then renders `100+ matches`, supports `maxResults` plus `offset` paging, and can include bounded context through `contextLines`. Long matching lines are centered around the match and rendered with explicit trim counts; long non-matching context lines are omitted with their character length. Search uses `ripgrep` when available and falls back to a Bun filesystem scanner with the same agent-facing output shape.

External repository path handling is intentionally strict: read/tree/search paths must remain inside the registered worktree after realpath resolution, symlink escapes are rejected, and search does not follow symlinks. Inspection tools do not expose arbitrary command execution or agent-driven writes; `external_repo_add` and `external_repo_update` only mutate the plugin-managed mirror/worktree cache.

## Container tools

`sandbox_exec` and `chroot_exec` use bundled container definitions by default. Container definitions can be overridden through `paths.containersDir` only in the trusted global `squad.json` configuration file.

The detailed helper container lifecycle is documented in [Containers](containers.md).

Runtime helper images are versioned by a short hash derived from the active bundled or configured `Containerfile`. If the active container definition changes, the next tool invocation automatically builds a new image revision before reuse.

After a new managed image revision is built successfully, the plugin prunes older managed image revisions for the same tool when no container is using them. This cleanup is post-build only; normal tool invocations do not scan image history.

Persistent helper containers are plugin-managed and carry ownership labels for tool and project/session identity. The plugin tracks sliding idle leases in its data directory and performs opportunistic cleanup on tool invocation. By default, unused helper containers become eligible for cleanup after 8 idle hours and are removed on a later `sandbox_exec` or `chroot_exec` invocation.

`chroot_exec` mounts the project root read-write at `/chroot`. Treat it as a powerful tool and keep destructive operations behind explicit approval.

## SearXNG

The SearXNG tools use bundled Compose assets unless overridden by trusted global configuration. The runtime helper generates `SEARXNG_SECRET` per plugin process and passes it to Compose through the environment; no static secret is committed.

## Security notes

- Prefer read-only tools for investigation.
- Use `sandbox_exec` for isolated experiments.
- Use `chroot_exec` only when writes to the project are intended.
- Keep `.env`, credentials, and generated state out of git.

Future work for configurable trust/protection overrides is tracked in [Config Protection Overrides](../todos/config-protection-overrides.md).

# Slash-command agents

Slash-command agents are registered as hidden OpenCode agents. You do not normally select them as your main assistant; you invoke them through commands.

## Inventory

| Command      | Display agent | Stable routing key | Model handler  | Purpose                                                               |
| ------------ | ------------- | ------------------ | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/beta`      | `beta`        | `squad/beta`       | `primary_beta` | Read-only second opinion on the current session.                      |
| `/configuru` | `configuru`   | `squad/configuru`  | `primary`      | Inspect and safely modify OpenCode or `opencode-squad` configuration. |
| `/retitler`  | `retitler`    | `squad/retitler`   | `primary`      | Rename the current OpenCode session or offer title suggestions.       |

`/beta` is for an independent second look. It is registered only when both the normal primary route and `squad/beta` resolve to concrete, different models.

This prevents a false sense of independent review. If both routes would use the same model, `/beta` stays hidden.

Route Beta through the `primary_beta` handler:

```json
{
  "models": {
    "handlers": {
      "primary": "@provider/main",
      "primary_beta": "@provider/second_opinion"
    }
  }
}
```

`/configuru` is the configuration assistant. It can inspect OpenCode and `opencode-squad` config locations, explain available configuration fields, and help shape safe edits.

Configuru has internal manuals and guardrails, but the public manual now exposes the main user-facing configuration surface in the [Configuration overview](configuration.md).

`/retitler` renames the current OpenCode session. It can either apply one chosen title directly or ask you to choose from suggestions.

# Primary agents

Primary agents are the agents you select for normal OpenCode collaboration. They share the same core safety and configuration blocks, but each one is tuned for a different style of work.

| `architect`       | `daedalus`       | `primary/architect`    | `primary`     | Architecture, RFCs, decomposition, system design, and solution shaping.                                       |
| `developer`       | `hephaestus`     | `primary/developer`    | `primary`     | Focused implementation with verification discipline.                                                          |
| `orchestrator`    | `sisyphus`       | `primary/orchestrator` | `coordinator` | Longer-running coordination, decomposition, and execution planning.                                           |

## Persona and display names

The `primary.persona` setting changes the role framing used in primary-agent prompts:

- `"professional"` uses `alpha`, `architect`, `developer`, and `orchestrator` framing.
- `"mythic"` uses `atlas`, `daedalus`, `hephaestus`, and `sisyphus` framing.

The `primary.useRoleName` setting controls whether display names follow the persona. Keep it `false` if you want stable visible names in the UI.

For model routing, prefer stable routing keys in `models.agents`:

```json
{
  "models": {
    "agents": {
      "primary/alpha": "@provider/main",
      "primary/orchestrator": "@provider/coordinator"
    }
  }
}
```

Most users should route primary agents through handlers instead:

```json
{
  "models": {
    "handlers": {
      "primary": "@provider/main",
      "coordinator": "@provider/main"
    }
  }
}
```

Use per-agent overrides only when one primary agent needs a different model from the others.

`beta` runs in primary mode internally so `/beta` can inspect the current session, but it is not a selectable primary agent. It is a hidden slash-command agent with its own routing behavior. See [Slash-command agents](agents-commands.md).

# Locations and precedence

`opencode-squad` merges configuration from defaults, files, and optional plugin tuple options. Later sources override earlier sources, except for fields that are intentionally limited to trusted global configuration.

## Global config

Global configuration belongs to the user and the current machine:

```text
$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/squad.json
```

When `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` is unset, OpenCode's normal config directory is used:

```text
~/.config/opencode/squad.json
```

Use the global file for personal preferences, user-wide behavior rules, model inventory, model selection strategy, and trusted local paths.

## Project config

Project configuration lives in the repository:

```text
<project>/.opencode/squad.json
```

Use project config for repository conventions, project-specific requirements, and project-specific model routing. Do not use it for secrets or machine-local path overrides.

## Plugin tuple options

OpenCode lets a plugin registration pass inline options. This can be useful when one OpenCode configuration file needs a local override at plugin load time:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    [
      "@geck-dev/opencode-squad",
      {
        "models": {
          "handlers": {
            "primary": "@provider/main"
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  ]
}
```

Prefer `squad.json` for settings that should be reused across sessions or shared with a project. Tuple options are best for narrow local experiments.

## Merge order

The runtime merges configuration in this order:

1. Built-in defaults.
2. Global `squad.json`, when present.
3. Project `.opencode/squad.json`, when present.
4. Plugin tuple options, when present.

Later sources override earlier sources. For example, a project can override a global model handler for that repository, and tuple options can override both for one plugin registration.

## Trusted-source exceptions

Some fields are accepted only from specific sources:

| Field                         | Accepted from  | Why                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `primary.userRequirements`    | Global config  | User-wide rules should be controlled by the user, not by a repository. |
| `primary.projectRequirements` | Project config | Repository rules should stay attached to the repository.               |
| `paths.dataDir`               | Global config  | A project must not redirect local plugin state.                        |
| `paths.containersDir`         | Global config  | A project must not redirect container helper definitions.              |

When a source tries to set a field outside its trust boundary, the runtime ignores that value and reports a diagnostic instead of silently applying it.

## Invalid or unsupported config

`squad.json` is strict JSON: no comments and no trailing commas. If a config file cannot be read, parsed, or validated, the plugin reports the diagnostic and continues with the remaining valid sources.

# Local paths

The `paths.*` fields control machine-local filesystem locations used by stateful plugin features and container helpers.

They are trusted fields. The runtime honors them only from global `squad.json`; project config and plugin tuple options are ignored for these fields.

## Why paths are global only

A repository should not be able to redirect your local plugin state or container definitions to attacker-chosen paths. Keeping `paths.*` global means these overrides come from your machine-level configuration, not from a project checkout.

## Data directory

`paths.dataDir` controls where stateful tools store plugin-managed data such as scratchpads, handoffs, and review context.

```json
{
  "paths": {
    "dataDir": "/absolute/path/to/opencode-squad-data"
  }
}
```

Runtime priority:

1. `$OPENCODE_DATA_DIR` environment variable.
2. `paths.dataDir` from global `squad.json`.
3. OpenCode config directory `data` folder.

Prefer the environment variable for temporary experiments. Use `paths.dataDir` when you want a persistent machine-level setting.

## Container asset directory

`paths.containersDir` points to custom container helper definitions:

```json
{
  "paths": {
    "containersDir": "/absolute/path/to/opencode-squad-containers"
  }
}
```

Most users should leave this unset. Set it only when you intentionally maintain custom container assets outside the package's bundled definitions.

## Rules

- Put `paths.*` only in global `squad.json`.
- Use absolute paths.
- Do not rely on `~` or shell variable expansion inside JSON strings.
- Confirm the directories exist and are writable before using them.
- Do not put secrets in these paths just because they are local.

# Retitler

The `retitler.*` fields configure the hidden agent behind the `/retitler` command. They affect session titles only. They do not change primary-agent behavior, model routing, or OpenCode's manual rename behavior.

## Defaults

| Field                   | Default | Effect                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `retitler.instructions` | `[]`    | Use only the built-in naming rules and one-off command text. |
| `retitler.suggestions`  | `false` | Pick one title and rename the current session directly.      |

## Naming instructions

Use `retitler.instructions` for recurring title rules:

```json
{
  "retitler": {
    "instructions": [
      "Use `<ticket-id> — <summary>` when a ticket ID is clearly present.",
      "Keep titles searchable; avoid slogans.",
      "Prefer the same language as the current conversation."
    ]
  }
}
```

Use the global file for personal naming preferences. Use project `.opencode/squad.json` for repository or ticket conventions.

For a one-time instruction, do not edit `squad.json`; pass it directly to the command:

```text
/retitler Use a short title with the ticket ID first
```

## Interactive suggestions

When `retitler.suggestions` is `true`, `/retitler` proposes three title options and asks you to choose one:

```json
{
  "retitler": {
    "suggestions": true
  }
}
```

This is useful when title style is subjective or when you want review before the session is renamed. Keep it `false` when you prefer `/retitler` to be a quick one-command action.

## Combined example

```json
{
  "retitler": {
    "instructions": ["Use issue keys when present.", "Keep titles factual and searchable."],
    "suggestions": true
  }
}
```

# Configuration overview

`opencode-squad` is configured with a strict JSON file named `squad.json`. You can keep the plugin almost configuration-free, or you can gradually add personal preferences, project rules, model routing, session-title behavior, and machine-local paths.

Start small. Add only the field group you actually need, then grow the file when the workflow asks for it.

## Configuration sources

Configuration can come from three user-controlled places:

| Source                         | Typical use                                                                             |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Global `squad.json`            | Personal preferences, model inventory, user-wide requirements, and trusted local paths. |
| Project `.opencode/squad.json` | Repository conventions and project-specific routing.                                    |
| Plugin tuple options           | One OpenCode config file that needs a local override while registering the plugin.      |

See [Locations and precedence](configuration-locations.md) for exact paths, merge order, and trust boundaries.

## Minimal valid file

A new file can start with only a schema reference:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/geck-dev/opencode-squad/main/schema/squad.schema.json"
}
```

The `$schema` field is optional at runtime, but useful in editors because it enables validation and completions.

Use the `raw.githubusercontent.com` URL above, not the normal GitHub `blob` page URL. Editors need the schema response body to be JSON; a URL such as `https://github.com/geck-dev/opencode-squad/blob/main/schema/squad.schema.json` points to GitHub's HTML file viewer and will usually not be accepted as a JSON schema.

## Supported field groups

| Area         | Page                                       | What it controls                                                                              |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `primary.*`  | [Primary agents](configuration-primary.md) | Primary-agent identity, persona, output style, user traits, and requirements.                 |
| `models.*`   | [Model routing](configuration-models.md)   | Provider pools, workload handlers, per-agent overrides, fallback, and availability selection. |
| `retitler.*` | [Retitler](configuration-retitler.md)      | Persistent behavior for the `/retitler` session-title command.                                |
| `paths.*`    | [Local paths](configuration-paths.md)      | Trusted machine-local directories for data and container assets.                              |

For copyable starting points, see [Configuration examples](configuration-examples.md).

## Practical rules

- Put personal preferences in global `squad.json`.
- Put repository conventions in project `.opencode/squad.json`.
- Keep `paths.*` global only; project files and tuple options cannot safely control machine-local paths.
- Omit `models.*` unless you want explicit model routing. Without it, OpenCode's current/default model can still be used.
- Prefer provider pools and handlers before per-agent model overrides.

## Example: small project config

This project-level file adds only repository rules:

```json
{
  "primary": {
    "projectRequirements": [
      "Use the package manager already used by this repository.",
      "Run the project check command before claiming completion."
    ]
  }
}
```

The rest of this section breaks the configuration surface into separate pages so each area can grow without turning the overview into a reference dump.

# opencode-squad manual

![OpenCode loads opencode-squad, which routes work to registered agents, tools, and container helpers.](assets/overview.svg)

## About OpenCode

[`OpenCode`](https://opencode.ai) is the agentic coding environment that runs this plugin. It gives you an AI partner inside your development workflow, connects that partner to models and project tools, and provides the runtime where agents can read code, reason about changes, and execute approved actions.

Without OpenCode, `opencode-squad` has nothing to attach to. The plugin is built to extend OpenCode rather than replace it: OpenCode provides the application, session, and tool system; `opencode-squad` adds a curated team of agents, safer helper tools, and project-level conventions on top.

## About our Squad

`opencode-squad` is an OpenCode plugin that loads a squad of primary agents, specialist subagents, and slash-command agents for practical software work.

The goal is not to make the assistant louder or more complicated. The goal is to make it easier to work in a structured way: primary agents handle broad collaboration, specialist agents take focused research or implementation tasks, and custom tools reduce repetitive setup around configuration, documentation, containers, and sandboxed execution.

The plugin also keeps safety boundaries visible. Configuration lives in a strict `squad.json` file, machine-local paths stay out of project config, and helper containers/sandboxes are used where isolation makes the workflow safer.

## Start here

- [Installation](installation.md) explains how to load the plugin locally or by package name.
- [Configuration](configuration.md) explains the `squad.json` configuration model and links to focused configuration pages.
- [Agents](agents.md) summarizes the bundled agents and routing keys.
- [Tools](tools.md) describes the custom tools and their operational risk levels.

## Design goals

- Keep the plugin usable with minimal configuration.
- Make model routing explicit and stable through named handlers.
- Keep machine-local paths and secrets out of project configuration.
- Give agents useful tools while preserving clear safety boundaries.

# Container execution

Container-backed tools let agents run commands without relying directly on the host shell. They are powerful tools, so the important distinction is whether the current project is mounted read-write.

## Tool inventory

| Tool                | Side effects                                                    | Purpose                                                                             |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sandbox_exec`      | Creates or reuses isolated sandbox state.                       | Runs commands in an isolated Fedora workspace.                                      |
| `chroot_exec`       | Executes with the project root mounted read-write at `/chroot`. | Runs commands against the current project in a Fedora container.                    |
| `container_runtime` | Read-only by default.                                           | Detects Docker/Podman, Compose support, SELinux state, and project container files. |

## `sandbox_exec`

Use `sandbox_exec` for experiments that do not need to mutate the project checkout:

- calculations
- quick scripts
- dependency-free repros
- testing an idea before touching files

The sandbox has its own workspace. It is useful when the answer needs command execution but not project writes.

## `chroot_exec`

Use `chroot_exec` when commands need the project mounted inside the container:

```text
/chroot
```

The mount is read-write. That makes `chroot_exec` appropriate for project checks, tests, builds, and intentional edits produced by commands. It also means destructive commands can damage the checkout.

Treat `chroot_exec` as a high-power tool:

- inspect before changing
- avoid destructive bulk operations without a dry run
- keep generated files and secrets out of Git
- prefer normal project validation commands over broad custom scripts

## Runtime helper lifecycle

The plugin uses bundled container definitions by default. They can be overridden only through trusted global configuration via `paths.containersDir`.

Helper images are versioned from the active container definition. When that definition changes, the next invocation builds a new managed image revision. Older managed revisions can be pruned after successful builds when they are no longer used.

Persistent helper containers use plugin ownership labels and idle leases. Cleanup is opportunistic during later tool invocations; unused helper containers become eligible after the configured idle window.

## When to use what

| Need                                         | Prefer                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Pure calculation or throwaway script         | `sandbox_exec`                                           |
| Run project tests or build commands          | `chroot_exec`                                            |
| Inspect available container runtime          | `container_runtime`                                      |
| Modify project files through a custom script | Dry-run first, then `chroot_exec` only with clear intent |

# External repositories

External repository tools let agents inspect upstream projects, framework source, or reference implementations without mixing that code into the current worktree.

The workflow is alias-based: register a repository once, then search and read it by alias.

## Tool inventory

| Tool                   | Side effects                                     | Purpose                                                  |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `external_repo_add`    | Clones or fetches plugin-managed Git state.      | Registers an external repository by alias.               |
| `external_repo_list`   | Reads plugin-managed state.                      | Lists repositories registered for the current project.   |
| `external_repo_search` | Read-only.                                       | Searches inside a registered repository.                 |
| `external_repo_read`   | Read-only.                                       | Reads a file or line range from a registered repository. |
| `external_repo_tree`   | Read-only.                                       | Shows a compact tree for a registered repository.        |
| `external_repo_status` | Read-only.                                       | Reports ref, commit, dirty state, and local path.        |
| `external_repo_update` | Fetches and checks out plugin-managed Git state. | Explicitly refreshes a registered repository.            |

## Basic workflow

1. Register the repository with a short alias.
2. Use `external_repo_tree` when you need orientation.
3. Use `external_repo_search` to find relevant symbols, filenames, or text.
4. Use `external_repo_read` for exact files and line ranges.
5. Use `external_repo_update` only when you intentionally want fresher reference code.

This keeps external code inspection explicit and repeatable.

## Storage model

External repositories are stored under the resolved plugin data directory:

```text
<dataDir>/external-repos/
  mirrors/<repo_hash>.git
  projects/<project_hash>/registry.json
  projects/<project_hash>/<alias>/worktree
```

Mirror caches are shared by repository URL hash. Worktrees and registries are scoped to the current project hash.

## Safety boundaries

The external repository tools do not expose arbitrary shell execution. They mutate only plugin-managed mirror/worktree state when registering or explicitly updating repositories.

Path handling is intentionally strict:

- reads, trees, and searches must stay inside the registered worktree
- symlink escapes are rejected
- search does not follow symlinks
- agents use aliases instead of arbitrary local paths

Use these tools when external source code is useful context, but should remain separate from the project you are editing.

# Local state

Local state tools store agent working context under the resolved plugin data directory. They are useful when information should persist across tool calls, subagents, reviews, or sessions without creating ad-hoc files in the project.

## Data directory

Stateful tools use this resolution order:

1. `$OPENCODE_DATA_DIR`
2. `paths.dataDir` from trusted global `squad.json`
3. `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/data` or `~/.config/opencode/data`

See [Local paths](configuration-paths.md) for the trust model.

| `scratchpad_patch`   | Writes plugin-managed state. | Applies exact replacement patches to scratchpad content. |

| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `handoff_prepare` | None.                        | Explains how to prepare concise persistent handoff content. |
| `handoff_write`   | Writes plugin-managed state. | Writes a persistent handoff for future sessions.            |

```text
<dataDir>/handoffs
```

They expose stable hashes, titles, timestamps, and project metadata so future sessions can recover context without relying on fragile conversation history.

| --------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |

## Git hygiene

State tools write to plugin-managed data directories, not the project checkout. Still, do not copy secrets, credentials, or generated state into Git-tracked files.

Agents receive only the tools their role needs. A read-oriented agent may receive diagnostics and search tools, while implementation or command agents may receive write-capable tools. This keeps the tool surface visible without giving every agent every capability.
